newsitem.title: USA: Clinton made U.S. decision on Bosnia arms - report.
newsitem.headline: Clinton made U.S. decision on Bosnia arms - report.

text.p: A top aide said President Bill Clinton personally made the controversial decision in 1994 not to oppose Iranian arms for Bosnian government forces, the Senate Intelligence Committee reported on Thursday.

The committee said the U.S. "green light" for Iran to provide arms to the Moslem-led government, at the same time that Washington publicly supported a U.N. embargo on such arms, created confusion among U.S. officials, particulary defence and intelligence officials who were not told of the change in policy.

"The strength in our democracy is that we do tell the truth ... We are honest. And this is not an honest policy," the committee's chairman, Sen. Arlen Specter, a Pennsylvania Republican, said at a press conference.
But the committee said it had reached no conclusion on whether the policy was an unauthorised U.S. covert operation.

Clinton administration officials acknowledged the Iran arms policy after it became public last spring but said they did not know if Clinton was involved in it. They said they feared at the time that Bosnia's government would collapse if it did not get the weapons.
"According to the national security adviser (Anthony Lake), the decision on how to respond to Croatia's April 1994 query was made by the president," the committee said.

Croatia's President Franjo Tudjman had asked if Washington would oppose Croatia's transshipment of arms primarily from Iran to Bosnian forces. According to Lake, Clinton made the decision to instruct U.S. diplomats to reply that they had "no instructions," the committee report said.

It said Clinton acted after a briefing by Lake and with the knowledge and support of senior State Department officials. U.S. Ambassador to Croatia Peter Galbraith had reported that any U.S. reply short of clear opposition would be seen by Croatia as a "U.S. green light," it added.
Congress' Republican leaders harshly criticised the policy as deceptive when it became public and ordered investigations in a run-up to Tuesday's presidential election.

A select House of Representatives committee report last month accused administration officials of making possibly criminal false statements about the policy, but minority Democrats dissented and said there were only contradictions in officials' memories of what happened.

The Senate committee's report made no such allegation. It also said it could not conclude that U.S. officials either encouraged Croatia, Iran or other countries to arm Bosnia's forces or took any action to aid the arms shipments.

But it said it was troubled by a memorandum saying that when a Croatian official told an unidentified senior U.S. official in 1995 that Croatia could not afford to stop the arms supplies, the U.S. official replied that Washington did not want them stopped.

The committee said it could draw no conclusion on whether U.S. agreement to inspect a shipment of missiles bound for Bosnia because of false rumours that they had chemical warheads amounted to U.S. support for the shipment.

The panel sided with former Central Intelligence Director James Woolsey in a dispute on whether he was clearly told of the U.S. policy change. Deputy Secretary of State Strobe Talbott testified to the committee that he told Woolsey at a meeting on May 5, 1994, "the essence" of the policy, but Woolsey said "I was never told that there had been any change in U.S. government policy."
The committee concluded that Woolsey was not told that an explicit decision had been made not to oppose Iran arms shipments to Bosnia.

It said in the report that it reached no conclusion on whether the U.S. policy was designed to influence Croatia and thus was an unauthorised covert operation or simply allowed events to proceed without U.S. influence.
Four committee Democrats dissented, saying the committee should have concluded it was not a covert operation.
